messages.subject: GUESS for calibrated data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christen,

Thanks for directing me to this page and the useful discussion. In response to my earlier query about a using weights=TRUE with the akde function, you suggested that to fix very slow computation times (and occasionally, non completion)  that I calibrate the data and use a smaller value of dt, suggesting 4 minutes. I have done this by working through the vignettes but have run into the following error at line 4 below. Any advice on what is preventing the estimation of GUESS greatly appreciated.

 > GUESS <- ctmm.guess(feralcat, CTMM=ctmm(error=TRUE), interactive=FALSE)

Error in `$<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, "SVF", value = 0) :  replacement has 1 row, data has 0

1.     dt <- c(20,96) %#% "minute"

2.     #dt <- 4 %#% "minute"

3.     vg.feralcat <- variogram(feralcat, dt=dt, fast=FALSE)  # for calibrated data using uere()

4.     GUESS <- ctmm.guess(feralcat, CTMM=ctmm(error=TRUE), interactive=FALSE)

5.     fitted.mods <- ctmm.select(feralcat, CTMM=GUESS,

level   = 1,

method  = "pHREML",

control = list(method="pNewton", cores = 2),

trace = TRUE,

verbose=TRUE)

6.     summary(fitted.mods)

David

messages.subject: Re: Parameterizing OU and OUf's sigma and tau
messages.subject_clean: Parameterizing OU and OUf's sigma and tau
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

Thank you so much for your rapid response and clarification! That is really helpful. I will use the ctmm.guess() to get initial parameters values to test with the OU and OUf models then. And just to clarify on the second question, any arguments specifying the bandwidth function should be written within the akde() command? Thank you!

Best,
Meredith

On Friday, February 28, 2020 at 10:57:53 AM UTC-5, Meredith VanAcker wrote:

> Dear Christen,
>
> I am trying to manually fit the OU and OUf models to my variogram and am having trouble understanding how to interpret the sigma and tau parameters in order to provide a range of values appropriate for my data. I have been testing out different values to see how it affects the fit to the variogram but I'm concerned that poorly fit values may impact the outcome of the weighted AKDE. It seems like sigma adjusts where the fitted line asymptotes - can you describe how tau changes the dynamics of the model fit?
>
> A secondary question is regarding the weighted AKDE. I have data that is duty cycled and would like to use the weighted option. Running the following AKDE : akde(one, M.OU, weights = TRUE) yesterday took ~ 2 hours. I am interested in testing out the various parameters in the bandwidth() argument to try to speed up the processing. Should the bandwidth() argument be run independently of the  akde() and saved as an object and then akde() references it automatically or does it need to be incorporated into the akde() argument?
>
> Thank you so much for your time! I am very excited to apply your package to my deer movement data!
>
> Best,
> Meredith
messages.body_snippet:
Dear Chris,

Thank you so much for your rapid response and clarification! That is really helpful. I will use the ctmm.guess() to get initial parameters values to test with the OU and OUf models then.

Chris

messages.subject: Re: problems with variogram calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gianluca,

By supplying drop=FALSE to as.telemetry(), you ensure that the output is a list of telemetry objects, even if there is only one. Then you are feeding the list object into variogram() and not the variogram object. The following works:

variogramma<-variogram(bacucco181614_t[[1]])

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: GUESS for calibrated data
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

"that this will provide an inaccurate estimate for very eccentric distributions" is with regards to forcing isotropic=TRUE to obtain a bandwidth scalar, rather than a matrix. I will clarify the documentation.

With a grid size for the one individual of 1 second (compared to 21-28 seconds), you should expect optimization to take 21-28 times longer to run as is. There are a few options to remedy this given in the documentation on bandwidth, for exactly when that happens: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/bandwidth.html

On the other hand, if the data contain some very tiny time intervals, say 1 second among hourly sampled data, then the default dt setting will create an excessively high-resolution discretization of time, which will also cause slowdown. In this case CTMM should contain an error model and dt can likely be increased to a larger fraction of the median sampling interval.

fast=FALSE uses exact times and has a computational cost as low as O(n^2), including O(n^2) function evaluations. With PC="direct" this method will produce a result that is exact to within machine precision, but with a computational cost of O(n^3). fast=FALSE,PC='direct' is often the fastest method with small datasets, where n ≤ O(1,000), but scales terribly with larger datasets.

Best,
Chris

Hi Chris,

Thank you for your help!! I looked over the location error on the vignette you provided. My lemurs are recorded in 10-minute sample intervals within ten months. I don't have calibration data, so I follow the directions on "Simultaneous fitting with uncalibrated data."  My DOF=68-84 which is still low for ten months of tracking; as shown below:

[1] "OUF anisotropic error"

$CI

area (hectares)        17.186252 21.517261 26.327624

τ[velocity] (minutes)   1.477568  5.703811 22.018245
speed (kilometers/day)  3.551830  5.103356  6.652662
error (meters)         13.988632 17.243720 20.492437

If I am reading this correctly, my lemur's position is 5 hours, with two crossings per day. The velocity is the average the animal travels with the same speed and direction; however, I notice intervals are wide instead of narrow. Lastly, the error is showing me the impact of location error, which is 17 meters? Is this correct, and is this a good model to use?

Thank you again for your help! I hope I am not confusing it too much,
Jelisa

messages.subject: Re: Location error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jelisa,

If the data are broken up, how many ~4-8 hour intervals are recorded in the data? You expect DOF[mean] and DOF[area] to be on the order of that amount. Long gaps in the data do not provide any information. The other thing I would consider is how well the variograms match.

The velocity autocorrelation timescale CIs are wide because the data are coarsely sampled relative to that scale and there is substantial location error.

14-20 meter error is plausible for GPS. Does your data record HDOP? That could be useful for an arboreal species. Also if you have the ability to collect some calibration data.

Best,
Chris
